  1. Elastin — the stretchy protein that lets skin and artery walls recoil; it degrades with age and in aneurysms.
  2. Elastography — ultrasound that maps tissue stiffness, e.g., FibroScan staging liver fibrosis.
  3. Solar elastosis — sun-damaged skin where elastic fibers break down, giving a leathery, weathered look.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Electrocardiogram (ECG) — tracing of the heart's electrical activity; the 12-lead you run on chest pain.
  2. Electroencephalogram (EEG) — records the brain's electrical activity to catch seizures.
  3. Electromyography (EMG) — measures muscle electrical signals to diagnose neuromuscular disease.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Pulmonary embolism (PE) — a clot plugging a lung artery; sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, and low sats.
  2. Fat embolism — fat globules plugging vessels after a long-bone fracture; a classic trauma complication.
  3. Embolic stroke — a clot travels from the heart (often A-fib) and plugs a brain artery.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Embryology — the study of how the embryo develops, the key to understanding birth defects.
  2. Embryonic period — weeks 3-8 of gestation when organs form and teratogens do the most damage.
  3. Embryo transfer — the IVF step where the embryo is placed into the uterus.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Hematemesis — vomiting blood, a red flag for an upper GI bleed like an ulcer or varices.
  2. Hyperemesis gravidarum — severe, dehydrating vomiting of pregnancy.
  3. Antiemetic — a drug that stops vomiting, like ondansetron (Zofran) you push for nausea.

Text: The word root {{c1::emmetr/o}} means {{c2::according to measure}}.
Back Extra:
WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Emmetropia — the eye's "just right" focus; light lands exactly on the retina, so no glasses are needed.
  2. Emmetropic — describing an eye that sees clearly at distance without any correction.
  3. Emmetropization — the process by which an infant's farsighted eye grows toward normal focus.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Encephalitis — inflammation of the brain itself; fever with altered mental status and seizures.
  2. Hepatic encephalopathy — brain dysfunction from liver failure, with confusion and a flapping tremor.
  3. Anencephaly — a neural tube defect where the brain fails to form; folate helps prevent it.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Gastroenteritis — inflammation of stomach and intestine; the "stomach bug" of vomiting and diarrhea.
  2. Enteral nutrition — feeding through the gut via an NG or PEG tube, as opposed to IV (parenteral).
  3. Necrotizing enterocolitis — life-threatening bowel inflammation in premature newborns.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Episiotomy — a surgical cut to the perineum during delivery to prevent a ragged tear.
  2. Episiorrhaphy — suture repair of the vulva/perineum after a delivery laceration.
  3. Episioplasty — surgical repair or reconstruction of the vulva.

Ex: erythrocyte = red blood cells that contain hemoglobin to carry oxygen

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Erythrocyte — the red blood cell that carries oxygen; a low count means anemia.
  2. Erythema migrans — the expanding red "bull's-eye" rash of early Lyme disease.
  3. Erythropoietin (EPO) — the kidney hormone that tells marrow to make more red cells.

Text: The word root {{c1::esthesi}} means {{c2::sensation or perception}}.
Back Extra:
WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Anesthesia — loss of sensation; local before suturing, or general for surgery.
  2. Paresthesia — the "pins and needles" tingling of a compressed or damaged nerve.
  3. Hyperesthesia — heightened, often painful skin sensitivity, seen with shingles or neuropathy.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Febrile — running a fever; charting "3 y/o presents febrile to 40°C."
  2. Febrile seizure — a convulsion triggered by a rapid fever spike in a young child.
  3. Febrile neutropenia — fever in a chemo patient with no white cells to fight it; an oncologic emergency.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Flexion — bending a joint; decorticate posturing is abnormal arm flexion in severe brain injury.
  2. Reflex — an automatic "bending back" response; the knee-jerk you test with a reflex hammer.
  3. Hepatic flexure — the sharp bend where the colon turns beneath the liver.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Foramen magnum — the large opening at the skull base where the brainstem passes; fatal if herniation compresses it.
  2. Patent foramen ovale (PFO) — a fetal heart opening that fails to close, linked to stroke in young adults.
  3. Intervertebral foramen — the opening where a spinal nerve exits; narrowing pinches it and causes radiculopathy.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Fracture — a break in a bone; the bread-and-butter of any orthopedic or trauma call.
  2. Comminuted fracture — bone broken into several fragments; think high-energy crush or MVC injuries.
  3. Refracture — a bone that breaks again at a previously healed site, often before full remodeling.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Gastritis — inflammation of the stomach lining; classic burning epigastric pain after NSAIDs or alcohol.
  2. Gastroenteritis — stomach and intestine inflammation; the vomiting-and-diarrhea 'stomach bug' you transport all the time.
  3. Gastrostomy (G-tube) — surgical opening into the stomach for feeding; you'll manage these in homebound and nursing-home patients.

Text: The word root {{c1::gest}} means {{c2::carry, produce, congestion}}.
Back Extra:
WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Gestation — the carrying of a pregnancy; 'gestational age' tells you how far along an OB patient is.
  2. Congestion — fluid backed up in tissue; pulmonary congestion is the wet crackles of CHF.
  3. Ingestion — the carrying of a substance into the body by mouth; a 'toxic ingestion' is a core poisoning and overdose call.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Hypoglycemia — low blood sugar; the diabetic found altered, diaphoretic, and confused who wakes up after dextrose.
  2. Hyperglycemia — high blood sugar; drives the fruity breath and deep breathing of DKA.
  3. Glycogen — the body's stored sugar in liver and muscle; released as glucose when blood sugar drops.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Diagnosis — knowing a condition 'through' its signs and tests; the whole point of your assessment.
  2. Prognosis — foreknowing how a disease will play out; what families ask about the most.
  3. Agnosia — loss of the ability to recognize objects, faces, or sounds despite intact senses; literally 'without knowing,' seen after stroke or brain injury.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Gynecology — the medical specialty for the female reproductive system; the 'GYN' in your OB/GYN calls.
  2. Gynecomastia — male breast tissue enlargement; a side effect of spironolactone and some liver disease.
  3. Gynecoid pelvis — the classic female-type pelvis shape, the roomiest inlet for vaginal delivery; contrast the android (male-type) pelvis.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Hematoma — a pooled collection of blood; the goose-egg on the scalp or the subdural after a fall.
  2. Hemorrhage — active bursting-forth of blood; the bleeding you control with pressure and tourniquets.
  3. Hematuria — blood in the urine; think kidney stones, trauma, or UTI.

Ex: hepatomegaly = enlargement of the liver

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Hepatitis — inflammation of the liver; the bloodborne types B and C are a needlestick and body-fluid exposure risk in EMS.
  2. Hepatomegaly — an enlarged liver you can palpate below the rib margin; seen in CHF (congestive hepatomegaly) and fatty liver disease.
  3. Hepatic encephalopathy — confusion from a failing liver not clearing toxins; the altered cirrhotic patient.
